title: The missing letter (Berakhot 4b)
hook: Psalm 145 runs through the alphabet but skips nun, the teachers say to avoid a verse about falling
carry: the Lord upholdeth all that fall

segments.voice: Yesterday, Psalm one hundred, the psalm of thanksgiving. Your line was thanks is the part meant to last. Did the chore feel different done gladly? Today, the psalm said three times a day, and the letter it leaves out. Day five hundred fifty-seven.
screen: `THANKS IS THE PART MEANT TO LAST.`

segments.voice: Psalm one hundred forty-five is an acrostic. Each verse begins with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet: alef, bet, gimel, and on down the line. The Talmud, in tractate Berakhot, makes a large promise about it: whoever says it three times a day, it says, is assured a place in the world to come. It sits at the heart of the prayer called Ashrei. But count the verses and something's off. The Hebrew alphabet has twenty-two letters. This psalm has twenty-one verses. One letter, partway through, is missing.
screen: `AN ALPHABET PSALM.` → `SAID THREE TIMES A DAY.` → `ONE LETTER IS MISSING.`

segments.voice: The missing letter is nun, the letter for the sound N. The Talmud, in tractate Berakhot, asks why. Rabbi Yochanan answers: because a terrible verse begins with nun. In the prophet Amos: fallen is the maiden Israel, she shall rise no more. Nafelah, fallen, starts with nun. So the psalmist, the teachers say, left the letter out rather than bring that word anywhere near a song of praise. Then another rabbi, Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak, adds the beautiful part. Even so, he says, David came back and caught them. Look at the very next verse, the one beginning with samech, the letter after nun. In the old Jewish translation: "The LORD upholdeth all that fall, and raiseth up all those that are bowed down." The word fall is right there. Not as a sentence, but as something caught. The fall is acknowledged, then immediately held. Now, what does the scholar hear? Among the Dead Sea Scrolls is a copy of this psalm that does have a nun verse: God is faithful in his words, and gracious in all his deeds. The ancient Greek translation has one too. So some scholars think a nun line once existed and dropped out of the traditional Hebrew text. The Talmud's reading doesn't depend on that question. It's a teaching about how to sing: you can leave a painful word unsaid, and still, in the next breath, say that the fallen are lifted.
screen: `NUN IS MISSING.` · `FALLEN, SHE SHALL RISE NO MORE.` · `THE NEXT VERSE CATCHES THEM.` · `A NUN LINE IN THE DEAD SEA SCROLLS.` · then, large: `THE MISSING LETTER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice what was left out kindly. Settle, and breathe. Think back over the last few weeks for a moment when someone could have said the hard thing, and didn't. A friend who didn't mention your mistake. A parent who let a bad grade go. Someone who changed the subject to spare you. Picture the word they didn't say. Then picture what they did instead: a hand on your shoulder, a joke, a lift home. That's the samech after the missing nun. The bell holds the time.
Nun. The letter for the sound N, left out of Psalm one hundred forty-five, the Talmud says, so the song never speaks of falling without catching.
Your line: the Lord upholdeth all that fall. Today, leave one hard word unsaid on purpose, and say something that lifts instead. Day five hundred fifty-seven.

howItsDone: Ashrei, built around Psalm 145, is said twice in the morning service and once in the afternoon service; in the morning it is the center of the verses of song.

fork.setup: you're writing an alphabet song of praise. the letter nun brings to mind a verse about Israel falling and never rising. what do you do?
options: use the verse anyway; it's honest.
leave the letter out, and catch the fallen in the next verse.
fork.reveal: that's the Talmud's reading: nun is left out, and the next verse says the LORD upholdeth all that fall.

original.note: Hebrew: the letter nun, the sound N, missing from Psalm 145.

trapdoor: what you thought: an alphabet psalm.
what it means: one letter is left out so the song never mentions falling without catching the fallen.
what a scholar hears: Berakhot 4b (Amos 5:2 and Psalm 145:14); the Qumran Psalms Scroll and the Septuagint preserve a nun verse, suggesting it dropped from the Masoretic text.

sources.quoted: The LORD upholdeth all that fall, and raiseth up all those that are bowed down.

notes: Psalm 145:14 quoted from JPS 1917 from memory; verify.
Berakhot 4b: Rabbi Yochanan's reason (Amos 5:2) and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's addition (David supported them with the holy spirit, Psalm 145:14); confirm attributions.
Amos 5:2 paraphrased ('fallen is the maiden Israel, she shall rise no more'); not quoted from JPS.
11QPs(a) and the Septuagint include a nun verse ('faithful is God in his words and gracious in all his deeds'); confirm wording of the paraphrase.
'Twice in the morning and once in the afternoon': Ashrei is said in Pesukei d'Zimra, after the Torah service/Uva l'Tziyon, and at Mincha; confirm.
